Title: Ailing State; Evolving Nation
NewsSubTitle: Javed Jabbar discusses the state of the nation at AKU
NewsSummary: When Javed Jabbar speaks, everyone is eager to listen to what he has to say. Such is the power in the words of the noted writer, intellectual and former information minister. It was no different at the Sixth Sense Forum lecture on January 28, 2014.
NewsContent:
When Javed Jabbar speaks, everyone is eager to listen to what he has to say. Such is the power in the words of the noted writer, intellectual and former information minister. It was no different at the Sixth Sense Forum lecture on January 28, 2014.

After an introduction by Dr Saad Shafqat, Jabbar took his place behind the rostrum and seeing the scanty attendance, made a quip that few would dare to make: “It is very sobering for any speaker who thinks all the seats are going to be taken.” But this is the quality of the man – the ability to speak the truth without making it sound horrible. “The sheer fact of being invited by the Sixth Sense Forum is a privilege. And I greatly admire the commitment to excellence that Aga Khan University represents.”
 
“Let’s proceed with the discussion Ailing State; Evolving Nation,” continued Jabbar. “I want to pose a question in the beginning. Do words make a difference? Yes, off course words make a difference. My preference is that our state is ailing. And off course I deliberately dropped the letter F which would have made it west’s most popular adverb to describe Pakistan. Failing state!”
 
A large part of the talk focused on the definition of terms like ‘state’ and ‘nation’ and the aetiology of nations. Jabbar spoke at length about how in many cases a nation evolved first and then adopted a state system to suit it. But the definition of what it means to be a nation is fluid, and Jabbar’s conclusion was that try as we might there is no substantive definition of a nation. At most nations were ‘imagined communities’ where people had the conviction that they shared common attributes.
 
Looking at history, Jabbar pointed out six different types of nation states: historic nations such as China and Egypt; migratory nations such as Australia; permutated states which arose out of a number of principalities coming together such as Germany and Italy; states created out of the break-up of other states such as Yugoslavia; post-colonial states which came about with the departure of colonial powers from Asia and religion based states such as Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
 
It was not until Pakistan was mentioned, that perhaps a few brows became knotted and few wrinkles appeared on foreheads – Pakistanis don’t usually take well to a discussion of their own existence – but Jabbar forged ahead.
 
“Two wings separated by a thousand miles of a hostile territory. No country in the world has been born with that structure. The idea that you could transcend geographic distance by sheer belief and conviction and sharing something whether its religion or values or dreams or whatever. It’s a tragedy that we couldn’t make it work. Were we an overnight state and an overnight nation? Very few nations and states have these dual achievements.
 
So we’re an overnight nation. Third of June; 10 weeks’ notice; but can you imagine a whole nation state being created at 10 weeks’ notice. Because of that 10 weeks’ notice period millions of people uprooted and panicked, one million slaughtered - died just because of that sheer arrogance.”
 
A short course in Indo-Pak history and the evolution of Pakistan in the post 1971 years followed. While lauding many of the private and public institutions of the country, Jabbar also made it a point to highlight the flaws found within the country.
 
An interesting aspect of the discussion revolved around the concept of a distinct Pakistani nationalism. Pakistaniat, “… at its most primitive level, it is expressed when Pakistan plays with India in a cricket match, you are rooting for Pakistan well that’s at a very primitive level but at other levels also. If we play the national anthem just now not only would we all stand up out of respect, obligation and even if we are sceptical, there would be a surge of emotion within us. It means that we have begun to relate to an identity and to a collectivism larger than the grievance and the shikayats and the frustrations that we feel 24 hours a day and that is an expression of Pakistaniat. But all of the Pakistaniat is not positive; there are some very negative facets also to our national identity; hate, obscurantism, misinterpretation of Islam, all that is part of Pakistaniat.”
 
Before ending his talk, Jabbar voiced his opinions on a variety of issues such as the importance of continuing with the democratic evolution of Pakistani politics and getting more people to vote, broadening of the tax net, promoting education as well as family planning. He pointed out that any viable change would have to come from each of us.
 
“It’s you and it’s me and it’s us and there’s no scope for saying ‘they’ and ‘them’. If we want to make this ailing state and to take it towards the culture of humanism … and you want to go towards a strong stable state, we have to do it together.”​
